newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ debt rallies with kiwi dlr to end firmer.
newsitem.headline: NZ debt rallies with kiwi dlr to end firmer.

text.p: Figures in brackets compare against previous day's close
FUTURES PHYSICAL YIELD (PCT)
90-DAY BILLS (SEP) 92.32 (PREV 92.26) 90-DAYS 8.40 (PREV 8.60)
OVERNIGHT CASH 8.25 PCT (PREV 8.60) US 5-YR 6.15 (PREV 6.12)
RBNZ MCI NZ/MCI 764.57 (PREV 772.24) Reuters NZ MCI -60 vs -53
* Short rates fall on firmer Kiwi, lower cash rate helps
* Bonds firm a touch, nervous ahead of Humphrey-Hawkins
* Currency seen falling further, set to push rates up again.
New Zealand debt markets staged a small rally on Monday in the wake of Friday's dramatic sell-off, but dealers said yields would rise again as soon as the currency resumed its downward journey.

"After such a big sell-off on Friday you're bound to get a bit of a correction. I think it was only really a corrective- type rally and there is probably still potential for bill yields to rise if the currency does weaken," said a bill dealer.
"There were a few fund managers buying in the one- and two- month area, with cash being a little bit lower today," he added.
The key 90-day bank bill rate fell 20 basis points to 8.40 percent and the cash rate eased back to 8.25 percent after the Kiwi dollar opened about 40 points firmer.
The bills had rocketed 90 points to 8.60 percent on Friday when the kiwi dollar was hammered by offshore investors, shedding over one U.S. cent.

Dealers said the general market expectation was for the kiwi to resume its downward path shortly, and for short rates to rise again in order to keep monetary conditions in touch with the Reserve Bank's preferences.

"With the MCI (Monetary Conditions Index) linking the two so closely, I suppose they've really got to," the bill dealer said, adding that despite Monday's rally, investors were still wary of getting back into the money market given the currency's outlook.

Bonds also fell across the curve, but not by as much, with the long bond yield ending seven points lower at 6.77 percent. "The bonds are a little bit stronger. We started off with a wee bit of offshore buying in the long bonds, then the currency holding its own and strengthening a bit this morning allowed the short end to come down a bit," said a senior bond dealer.
The Australian bond market had also rallied which had helped underpin the New Zealand market.
He said there was some apprehension in the market ahead of Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan's Humphrey-Hawkins testimony on Tuesday and Wednesday (U.S. time).
"If that gets out of the way alright, then we've got room to go down a little bit more (in yield) I think."
He said offshore investors were more interested in New Zealand's long-dated assets than its short rates at the moment.
